questions.question: In the course's network terminology, a path is a sequence of distinct edges joining consecutive vertices. Which description defines a cycle?
options: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex.
A route back to its start that may reuse edges.
A path that visits every vertex of the network.
A sequence of edges in which no vertex appears twice.

questions.question: In an undirected network, a route starts at $A$, uses the edge $A\text{-}B$ to reach $B$ and returns to $A$ along the same edge. Is the route $A\text{-}B\text{-}A$ a cycle?
options: Yes, because it starts and ends at the same vertex.
No, because it uses the single edge $A\text{-}B$ twice.
Yes, it is a cycle of two edges, twice as long as $A\text{-}B$.
Only if the edge is undirected, so that it may be reused.

questions.question: An undirected network contains the triangles $B\text{-}C\text{-}D$ and $B\text{-}E\text{-}F$, which share only the vertex $B$. In the course's convention, is the closed route $B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}B\text{-}E\text{-}F\text{-}B$ a cycle?
options: Yes, since its six edges are distinct and it closes at $B$.
No, since the vertex $B$ is visited in the middle as well.
No, it is two cycles that only happen to be written together.
Yes, but only because it visits every vertex of the network.

questions.question: In an undirected network, vertex $E$ is an endpoint of exactly one edge, $D\text{-}E$. Can the edge $D\text{-}E$ lie on a cycle?
options: Yes, if the cycle is long enough to come back to $E$.
Yes, if $D$ lies on a cycle, which then extends to $E$.
Yes; every edge of a network lies on some cycle.
No; leaving $E$ would reuse the edge $D\text{-}E$.

questions.question: A directed network has the edges $A\to B$, $B\to C$ and $A\to C$, each usable only in its direction. Do these three edges form a directed cycle?
options: Yes, they join $A$, $B$, $C$ in a triangle.
Yes, since any three edges on three vertices close up.
No; from $C$ no edge leads back into $A$ to close it.
Yes, if $A\to C$ is used once in the reverse direction.

questions.question: An undirected network has vertices $A,B,C,D$ and edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$ and $B\text{-}D$. Which route is a cycle in this network?
options: $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}D\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}D\text{-}B\text{-}A$
$B\text{-}C\text{-}D$

questions.question: An undirected network has edge lengths $A\text{-}B=4$, $B\text{-}C=3$, $C\text{-}D=5$, $D\text{-}A=2$ and $A\text{-}C=6$. What is the length of the cycle $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}A$?

An undirected network has vertices $A,B,C,D$ and edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$ and $B\text{-}D$. How many different cycles does it contain, counting a cycle once whatever its start vertex and direction?
An undirected network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $B\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}E$ and $D\text{-}F$. Which statement about cycles in this network is correct?
options: It has a cycle, since the route $B\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}D\text{-}B$ returns to $B$.
It has no cycle, since no route returns without reusing an edge.
It has a cycle, since $B$ and $D$ each have three edges and are joined by an edge.
It has no cycle, since every vertex has an odd number of edges, and a cycle needs even ones.

questions.question: An undirected network is the chain $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E$ (edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}E$). The edge $B\text{-}E$ is added. Which cycle does the enlarged network now contain?
options: $A\text{-}B\text{-}E\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}A$
$B\text{-}E\text{-}B$
$B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}B$

questions.question: In an undirected network, the edge $u\text{-}v$ lies on a cycle, and this one edge is removed. What can be said about the vertices $u$ and $v$ afterwards?
options: They remain joined through the rest of the cycle's edges.
They become separated, since their edge is gone.
They remain joined only if the cycle has at least four edges.
They remain joined only if another edge joins them directly.

questions.question: In an undirected network, a new edge is added between two existing vertices $u$ and $v$. When does the enlarged network contain a cycle through the new edge?
options: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ were already joined by a path.
Exactly when $u$ and $v$ were already joined by an edge.
Exactly when $u$ or $v$ already lay on some cycle.
Always, because a new edge always closes a route.

questions.question: An undirected network has the edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$ and $C\text{-}A$, of lengths $1$, $2$ and $3$. A student writes the routes $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A$, $B\text{-}C\text{-}A\text{-}B$ and $A\text{-}C\text{-}B\text{-}A$. Which statement about the edges and lengths of these routes is correct?
options: They use different edges, as the edges are listed in different orders.
Two use the same edges, but $A\text{-}C\text{-}B\text{-}A$ runs them the wrong way round.
They use the same edges, but their lengths differ with the start vertex.
They use the same three edges once each, so each has length $1+2+3=6$.

questions.question: Two-way roads between depots have lengths $A\text{-}B=2$, $B\text{-}C=3$, $C\text{-}A=6$, $A\text{-}D=4$ and $D\text{-}B=1$. A courier wants the shortest round trip that starts and ends at depot $A$ and uses no road twice. How long is it?
A directed network has the edges $A\to B$, $B\to C$, $C\to A$, $C\to D$ and $D\to B$, each usable only in its direction. Which route is a directed cycle?
options: $B\to D\to C\to B$
$A\to B\to C\to D\to A$
$B\to C\to D\to B$
$C\to D\to B\to C\to A$

questions.question: An undirected network consists of the triangle $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A$ and the square $C\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}F\text{-}C$, which share only the vertex $C$. What is the smallest number of edges whose removal leaves no cycle at all?
For a network with finitely many vertices, consider the condition that every vertex is an endpoint of at least two edges. How is this condition related to the network containing a cycle?
options: It is required for a cycle, but does not guarantee one.
It is both required for and enough for a cycle.
It neither guarantees a cycle nor is required for one.
It guarantees a cycle, but a cycle can exist without it.

questions.question: In an undirected network, two paths join the vertices $u$ and $v$ and have no edge in common, although they may pass through some common vertices. What follows?
options: A cycle exists only if the two paths share no vertex except $u$, $v$.
A cycle exists only if $u$ and $v$ are joined by an edge.
No cycle need exist; they are just two parallel routes.
Going out along one and back along the other is a cycle.

questions.question: Four tasks $P,Q,R,S$ have precedence arrows $P\to Q$, $Q\to R$, $R\to S$, $S\to Q$ and $P\to S$, where $X\to Y$ means that $X$ must be finished before $Y$ starts. Which tasks lie on a directed cycle, so that they cannot all be put in a valid order?
options: $P$, $Q$ and $S$
No tasks; the arrows contain no cycle
$Q$, $R$ and $S$
All four tasks $P,Q,R,S$

questions.question: Two different two-way roads join towns $A$ and $B$, of lengths 3 and 5; further roads are $A\text{-}C$ of length 3 and $C\text{-}B$ of length 3. Each road is a separate edge. What is the length of the shortest cycle through $A$?
